messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 65
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Retail Worker
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 60

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit, Distraction: I distract myself with something else, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame is a 65-year-old married man who emigrated from Africa many years ago and now works in retail, spending long days on the sales floor helping customers, straightening shelves, and watching the automatic doors slide open and shut. He traces the beginning of his current difficulties to a natural disaster that struck without warning and altered his sense of safety in a way that still feels immediate. When the disaster hit, he was indoors with other people, and what stays with him most is the experience of needing to get out while the building around him no longer felt dependable. He remembers the confusion of looking for a way out, trying to judge where to move, and feeling with total clarity that survival depended on noticing danger quickly and staying close to an exit. Even now, when he speaks about it, the scene does not come back as an ordinary recollection. It comes as a sequence that replays in full, “like a film,” with such force that he feels himself back inside that moment rather than remembering something finished.

In the weeks after the disaster, Kwame had expected the fear to settle once normal life resumed, but he found that ordinary indoor spaces no longer felt ordinary. Entering any room, he would automatically search for exits before he took in anything else. He had come to believe that this was simply what a sensible person had to do in a dangerous world. If he sat down at a restaurant, attended church, or went to a family gathering, he was most comfortable when he could position himself near a door. The farther he was from an exit, the less able he felt to relax. He noticed himself constantly checking his surroundings for signs that something might go wrong, not because anything specific was happening in the present, but because being off guard felt intolerable. In his mind, the lesson of the disaster was unmistakable: the world can turn threatening at any moment, and only people who stay alert have a chance.

These habits became especially visible at work. In the retail store, Kwame is aware of entrances, stockroom doors, emergency exits, and the flow of customers almost as soon as he steps onto the floor. If a manager asks him to work in an interior section of the store away from the main doors, he feels a quiet rise in tension and finds himself glancing repeatedly toward the nearest exit route. He distracts himself to get through these shifts, throwing himself into folding clothes, reorganizing displays, or focusing intensely on small tasks so he does not have to sit with the sense that something could happen. Even with that effort, he remains watchful. Coworkers may simply see him as serious or unusually alert, but to Kwame it feels necessary, a basic rule for getting through the day.

At night, the same stance follows him home. Sleep has become difficult not because he does not feel tired, but because lying down means loosening the vigilance he depends on. He has difficulty falling asleep because part of him feels he needs to stay alert. When he is in bed, his mind can begin replaying the disaster with vivid force, and what frightens him most is how little distance there is between then and now. The memory does not feel safely stored in the past. It feels present, as if the danger is happening again in real time. He has come to believe that he has changed permanently for the worse since the disaster, that he is no longer the man who could move through the world with ease or trust that a building, a room, or a routine day at work is simply safe.

Over months and then years, this way of living has narrowed his life. He still works and remains committed to his marriage, but much of his energy goes into staying on guard, scanning, positioning, and mentally managing himself. His wife has seen how hard it is for him to settle even in familiar places, and she has noticed how quickly he studies a room instead of enjoying it. Kwame himself is troubled by how relentless it feels. He does not experience his alertness as a quirk; he is certain he has to be on guard all the time. Recently, after another period of poor sleep and repeated episodes in which the disaster replayed so strongly that he felt he was back in it, he agreed to seek help. What brings him now is not uncertainty about whether he is suffering—he knows he is—but fear that this is his life from here on: always watching, always braced, always one step from danger. What he hopes, cautiously, is not to forget what happened, but to find some way to live in the present without feeling that every room must be survived.
